item.title: Amazon gives Wall Street mixed financial picture in earnings report
item.description: E-commerce company posts high cloud computing sales but gives a cautious sales forecast for the fourth quarter Amazon offered a mixed picture of its financial health on Thursday in its quarterly earnings report. The e-commerce company gave a cautious sales forecast for the current fourth quarter, which encompasses the critical holiday shopping period, after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations. item.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
item.description: null The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release . Wiseman announced his transition to "astronaut emeritus" alongside Artemis II pilot Victor Glover in September. Glover, subsequently, accepted a full-time role as executive advisor to the president of his alma mater , California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly). Artemis II mission specialists, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen , also made the decision to step away from their spaceflight careers. Hansen announced his career change in July, and has since entered into reservist duty with the Royal Canadian Air Force. Koch, more recently, was appointed as NASA's acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. The quartet launched aboard NASA's Orion capsule on April 1, and completed a 10-day flight around the far side of the moon and back. Their mission took them further from Earth than any crewed spaceflight in history, and captured the attention of millions, who were captivated by the astronauts' incredible views and their ability to demonstrate the best traits of humanity, even while being the four people farthest from it. The mission served as a stepping stone in NASA's Artemis program which aims to return astronauts to the surface of the moon and eventually establish a permanent base there. NASA is targeting mid-2027 for Artemis III as a flight test with Orion and the two Artemis lunar lander spacecraft (SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon ). If everything goes according to plan, that mission will pave the way for Artemis IV, and the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028. From left: The Artemis II crew — NASA astronaut Christina Koch, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, and NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover — take time out for a group hug inside the Orion spacecraft on April 6, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) A Baltimore native, Wiseman is a retired U.S. Navy captain who served as an aviator and test pilot before joining NASA's astronaut corps in 2009. He launched to space for the first time on the on the Soyuz TMA-13M mission to the International Space Station (ISS). item.content:encoded: null The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release . Wiseman announced his transition to "astronaut emeritus" alongside Artemis II pilot Victor Glover in September. Glover, subsequently, accepted a full-time role as executive advisor to the president of his alma mater , California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly). Artemis II mission specialists, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen , also made the decision to step away from their spaceflight careers. Hansen announced his career change in July, and has since entered into reservist duty with the Royal Canadian Air Force. Koch, more recently, was appointed as NASA's acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. The quartet launched aboard NASA's Orion capsule on April 1, and completed a 10-day flight around the far side of the moon and back. Their mission took them further from Earth than any crewed spaceflight in history, and captured the attention of millions, who were captivated by the astronauts' incredible views and their ability to demonstrate the best traits of humanity, even while being the four people farthest from it. The mission served as a stepping stone in NASA's Artemis program which aims to return astronauts to the surface of the moon and eventually establish a permanent base there. NASA is targeting mid-2027 for Artemis III as a flight test with Orion and the two Artemis lunar lander spacecraft (SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon ). If everything goes according to plan, that mission will pave the way for Artemis IV, and the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028. From left: The Artemis II crew — NASA astronaut Christina Koch, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, and NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover — take time out for a group hug inside the Orion spacecraft on April 6, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) A Baltimore native, Wiseman is a retired U.S. Navy captain who served as an aviator and test pilot before joining NASA's astronaut corps in 2009. He launched to space for the first time on the on the Soyuz TMA-13M mission to the International Space Station (ISS). He spent 165 days in orbit serving as part of ISS Expeditions 40 and 41, and completed two spacewalks totaling nearly 13 hours. Before his selection for Artemis II, Wiseman worked as NASA's chief astronaut, overseeing crew readiness, astronaut assignments and flight safety from Dec. 2020 - Nov. 2022. As JPL's new deputy director, Wiseman will serve under Director Dave Gallagher, helping oversee "strategic leadership, stewardship, and continuous improvement of laboratory operations," according to the JPL release. JPL is a federally funded research and development center specializing in robotic space exploration. The lab is responsible for some of NASA's most recognizable planetary missions, including the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers, Europa Clipper and the Voyager probes. JPL also operates NASA's Deep Space Network, which provides continuous communications with spacecraft throughout the solar system. "I've explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the sun disappear behind the moon from deep space," Wiseman said. "But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation.”

item.title: Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat
item.description: If you want to ask AI a question and watch the conversation go up in virtual flames when you're done, there's a new Mac app for that. Howler is an open-source app from a Chinese developer going by Aries Zhou, and it takes incognito mode AI questions to a new level by making them graphically interesting and easy to access right from the desktop of a macOS device. Anyone familiar with the Harry Potter series is likely to know where the name comes from - Howlers are letters that scream in recipients’ faces and then burst into flames, destroying themselves, which is the exact same thing the prompts ostensibly do once a user taps the Escape key. The Howler app displays a parchment-esque letter on the screen whenever the user presses Option+H, complete with a little wax seal that shows a letter representing their chosen model. Responses to queries are written out “at a hand’s pace,” per Howler’s website, first in glowing gold that settles to a sepia-toned print. “Besides needing translation at any time, I often want to look up a concept or learn about an event on the fly, without wanting to switch to a browser or open a separate session in Chat,” Zhou wrote in a comment on his Hacker News post showing off the applet. “So I made Howler, dedicated to Harry Potter fans, always there when you call, burning after reading.” The biggest catch to using Howler is that setting it up involves either using an AI service that can run commands, like Claude Code or another coding agent, or running the configuration commands manually. The recommended method involves pasting a setup prompt into the agent's input field. Once set up, Howler can connect to supported AI models using an API key, or to compatible models running locally. Howler’s website states that the API key never enters the chat and is stored in the macOS Keychain for safety. In addition to the API key for the chosen model staying local and not being printed, Howler is described on its website as only storing messages in memory with no history, sending requests straight to the chosen AI service and never through a relay, keeping no logs, and only connecting to an outside service to check for updates - and even that feature can be disabled. It’s a handy tool for those who want to ask AI questions without leaving a chat history on their Mac – like trying to remember the name of that damn function you’re supposed to have down by now, or whether Memorial Day or Labor Day is the one in the fall. Just don’t assume the AI provider won’t retain a record of the exchange. “Unlike regular conversations, it doesn't take up your conversation list, and you don't have to think about cleaning it up or archiving it afterward,” Zhou explained. “It's only for handling your sudden flashes of inspiration or a moment of confusion.” And it does it with panache - sure, it’s just an interface for an AI model one could find elsewhere, but it’s easily conjured, dismissed with a snap, and is open source, to boot. You can find Howler

item.title: Astronauts deploy solar array on 100th US spacewalk by International Space Station crew members
item.description: null Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost. Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain. NASA astronaut Anil Menon carries a rolled-up solar array to the site where it will be deployed while riding on the end of the Canadarm robotic arm during a spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) Once outside, Menon and Kutryk worked on unbolting the ISS roll-out solar array ( iROSA ) from a temporary stowage platform. The 10-by-2-by-4-foot (3-by-0.6-by-1.2-meter) rolled-up assembly was delivered to the space station inside the unpressurized trunk of SpaceX 's Dragon cargo capsule earlier this month, on the company's 35th ISS resupply mission for NASA. Menon then secured himself at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and carried the 750-pound (340-kilogram) iROSA to the space station's port side, where he and Kutryk next installed it on the 2A electrical power channel. Kutryk made his way to the worksite along the station's backbone truss. Using bolts to mount the IROSA in place and connecting its electrical cables to tie it into the station's power system (during a night pass, out of safety concerns), the array was ready to be extended. No motor was needed to deploy the iROSA to its 63-foot (19-m) length. The potential energy held by the assembly's rolled-up carbon composite booms was enough to fully unroll the panel. "And we see the iROSA deploying now," reported Mission Control four hours and 23 minutes into the spacewalk. About 12 minutes later, the array had fully extended, draping over about half of the larger but less capable legacy panel on the P4 truss. The station's eight original arrays are showing degraded power output as they have exceeded their 15-year design life. The iROSAs, when used in tandem with their older counterparts, have increased the station's power supply by 20% to 30%. The additional power is needed to support ongoing and planned station operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit , which is currently scheduled for 2030. Having worked ahead of their schedule, Menon and Kutryk removed some of the beams holding the final iROSA in place on its temporary platform and rotated two launch locks that were used in its delivery on Dragon . Thursday's EVA was the 100th U.S. outing from the space station without a now-retired space shuttle docked to the complex. Overa

Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain. NASA astronaut Anil Menon carries a rolled-up solar array to the site where it will be deployed while riding on the end of the Canadarm robotic arm during a spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) Once outside, Menon and Kutryk worked on unbolting the ISS roll-out solar array ( iROSA ) from a temporary stowage platform. The 10-by-2-by-4-foot (3-by-0.6-by-1.2-meter) rolled-up assembly was delivered to the space station inside the unpressurized trunk of SpaceX 's Dragon cargo capsule earlier this month, on the company's 35th ISS resupply mission for NASA. Menon then secured himself at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and carried the 750-pound (340-kilogram) iROSA to the space station's port side, where he and Kutryk next installed it on the 2A electrical power channel. Kutryk made his way to the worksite along the station's backbone truss. Using bolts to mount the IROSA in place and connecting its electrical cables to tie it into the station's power system (during a night pass, out of safety concerns), the array was ready to be extended. No motor was needed to deploy the iROSA to its 63-foot (19-m) length. The potential energy held by the assembly's rolled-up carbon composite booms was enough to fully unroll the panel. "And we see the iROSA deploying now," reported Mission Control four hours and 23 minutes into the spacewalk. About 12 minutes later, the array had fully extended, draping over about half of the larger but less capable legacy panel on the P4 truss. The station's eight original arrays are showing degraded power output as they have exceeded their 15-year design life. The iROSAs, when used in tandem with their older counterparts, have increased the station's power supply by 20% to 30%. The additional power is needed to support ongoing and planned station operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit , which is currently scheduled for 2030. Having worked ahead of their schedule, Menon and Kutryk removed some of the beams holding the final iROSA in place on its temporary platform and rotated two launch locks that were used in its delivery on Dragon . Thursday's EVA was the 100th U.S. outing from the space station without a now-retired space shuttle docked to the complex. Overall, it was the 285th spacewalk in support of ISS assembly, maintenance and upgrades, including 66 EVAs out of the Russian segment of the station and 119 by visiting shuttle crews. The seventh and penultimate International Space Station (ISS) roll-out solar array (IROSA) is seen unfurling after its installation by two spacewalkers on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The first U.S. spacewalk outside of the Quest airlock was made by Expedition 4 crewmates Carl Walz and Daniel Bursch on Feb. 20, 2002. The 5-hour-and-47-minute EVA mostly tested Quest's systems and completed "housekeeping chores." "Being outside, I can say it is always sunny in space," said Menon at the conclusion of Thursday's EVA. "I find it incredible what we have been able to do to provide new solar arrays to the space station. In fact, we have been ... doing complex operations like this for over 26 years." "This is USOS [United States Operating Segment] EVA 100, which is an incredible milestone. I think it really signifies how much we have done," he said. This was Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. Menon has now logged 26 hours and 31 minutes working in the vacuum of space during his current stay on the space station. Kutryk is the fifth Canadian astronaut to conduct an EVA. He and Menon are scheduled for another EVA on Nov. 5, when they are expected to install the eighth and final iROSA, completing the five-year process to upgrade the station's power supply.

item.title: 'Crystal Lake' is great, but nothing tops the space horror shenanigans of 'Jason X'
item.description: null Peacock's "Crystal Lake" takes the story of the Voorhees family back to the beginning. It's a full-circle moment revisiting Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini), who's the real star of 1980's "Friday the 13th" and the catalyst for all the murder and mayhem. While it's a welcome shake-up to the timeline of the horror franchise, nothing tops the originality of the slasher-in-space spectacle known as "Jason X". It was 2001, and the "Friday the 13th" franchise had hit a bit of a snag. Audiences had seen Jason Voorhees go everywhere from Crystal Lake to Manhattan and Hell, but where else could this hockey-masked killer go? Screenwriter Todd Farmer had the answer: space . "Jason X" says the quiet part out loud: Jason (Kane Hodder) can't die. In this movie, we find Jason being held at the Crystal Lake Research Facility in 2010. The head of the facility, Rowan LaFontaine (Lexa Doig), wants to put him in a cryogenic chamber, but the government has other plans for him. Things go as well as can be expected, with Jason freeing himself and slaughtering military men like they're pancakes at a buffet. Fortunately, Rowan manages to lure Jason into a cryogenic chamber as he stabs her, leaving them both frozen in time. (Image credit: New Line Cinema / Crystal Lake Entertainment) Fast forward to 2455, when a group of space explorers — led by Professor Brandon Lowe (Jonathan Potts) — discover the research facility and the frozen bodies. They bring Rowan and Jason on board their ship, the Grendel . While they believe Jason to be dead, they're able to revive Rowan using nanotechnology. As it so happens, Jason isn't dead at all (what a shocker); he was just catching up on some sleep and dreaming about stuffing teens in sleeping bags and whacking them against each other. He rises from his slumber and goes on a killing spree in the spaceship. item.dc:creator: Sergio Pereira
item.content:encoded: null Peacock's "Crystal Lake" takes the story of the Voorhees family back to the beginning. It's a full-circle moment revisiting Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini), who's the real star of 1980's "Friday the 13th" and the catalyst for all the murder and mayhem. While it's a welcome shake-up to the timeline of the horror franchise, nothing tops the originality of the slasher-in-space spectacle known as "Jason X". It was 2001, and the "Friday the 13th" franchise had hit a bit of a snag. Audiences had seen Jason Voorhees go everywhere from Crystal Lake to Manhattan and Hell, but where else could this hockey-masked killer go? Screenwriter Todd Farmer had the answer: space . "Jason X" says the quiet part out loud: Jason (Kane Hodder) can't die. In this movie, we find Jason being held at the Crystal Lake Research Facility in 2010. The head of the facility, Rowan LaFontaine (Lexa Doig), wants to put him in a cryogenic chamber, but the government has other plans for him. Things go as well as can be expected, with Jason freeing himself and slaughtering military men like they're pancakes at a buffet. Fortunately, Rowan manages to lure Jason into a cryogenic chamber as he stabs her, leaving them both frozen in time. (Image credit: New Line Cinema / Crystal Lake Entertainment) Fast forward to 2455, when a group of space explorers — led by Professor Brandon Lowe (Jonathan Potts) — discover the research facility and the frozen bodies. They bring Rowan and Jason on board their ship, the Grendel . While they believe Jason to be dead, they're able to revive Rowan using nanotechnology. As it so happens, Jason isn't dead at all (what a shocker); he was just catching up on some sleep and dreaming about stuffing teens in sleeping bags and whacking them against each other. He rises from his slumber and goes on a killing spree in the spaceship. It's not the slasher-in-space concept alone that elevates this flick (it's pretty much a running joke that every horror franchise ends up in space eventually). No, it's the brave (and honestly wild) turns that Jason X takes towards the end. (Image credit: New Line Cinema / Crystal Lake Entertainment) They turn the movie's android KM-14 (played by Lisa Ryder of "Andromeda" fame) into a Rambo-esque action hero in the third act, whereby she annihilates Jason with a combination of hokey martial arts moves and ridiculously overpowered weapons. Sadly, KM-14 makes a critical mistake: she obliterates the silent but violent killer near the medical station where the nanites reside. Not only does Jason get rebuilt bigger and stronger than before, but he's also now a cyborg with a brand-new metal mask and armor. Needless to say, "Jason X" fully commits to every eccentric idea and bonkers premise. From the "Kung Pow"-before-"Kung Pow" face-off between KM-14 and Jason to the totally ludicrous and gory kills that border on implausible, this is the "Friday the 13th" movie that you'd dream up after eating too much cheese at midnight. Most importantly, though, it's never afraid to embrace the shlock and humor that's evidently part of its DNA. "Jason X" is a B-movie through and through, and it waters its roots to grow wilder rather than hide or trim them down. (Image credit: New Line Cinema / Crystal Lake Entertainment) For instance, when Condor (Steve Lucescu) fights against Jason, he throws a bunch of stiff attacks at Crystal Lake's most famous citizen. However, Jason simply pushes him into a giant drill that's conveniently placed there (where are the health and safety regulations on the Grendel ?!). That isn't even the best part here, because when Elijah Brodski (Peter Mensah) asks the others about Condor's status, he gets met with the sensational line, "He's screwed." How this movie didn't get an Oscar nomination for best screenplay is still a mystery… It would also be remiss to not mention the greatest kill in "Jason X" — and maybe the "Friday the 13th" franchise as a whole — as Jason freezes Adrienne's (Kristi Angus) head in liquid nitrogen then shatters it against the counter. It's a scene so iconic that even the "MythBusters" became fascinated with this idea and had to try it themselves, though without actual human heads being used, of course. (Image credit: New Line Cinema / Crystal Lake Entertainment) What "Jason X" represents is a different time in Hollywood, when studios and filmmakers weren't afraid to take outlandish risks with their franchises. Think about it: What else was there left for "Friday the 13th" to do? Let Jason murder more teens who cross his path? Instead of just repeating the same formula over and over again, these filmmakers decided to think outside of the box and venture into an unexpected direction. Whether you like it or not, you have to appreciate the commitment to trying something new and reinventing the franchise. When all is said and done, "Crystal Lake" will be remembered as a more cerebral examination of the Voorhees family, but "Jason X" might be seen as the pinnacle of creativity in the series that's never going to be reached again. It's so goofy and silly, but the concept of taking an unkillable killer, chucking him into space, and making him a cyborg deserves a standing ovation. We're once again left wondering: Why aren't we making horror movies like this anymore? Want to relive the madness of "Jason X" for Halloween? You can catch it on Philo , and you can watch the new Jason/Friday the 13th prequel "Crystal Lake" on Peacock . item.title: Startup wants to make AI agents safe for DevOps duty
item.description: Vera Platforms, a startup founded by researchers at the University of Michigan, believes there's a way to make agents trustworthy enough to handle DevOps. DevOps, which focuses on how software gets deployed and operated, is a particularly unforgiving affair. While AI agents have some leeway to make mistakes and correct errors as they generate code and work through a prompt, it's an entirely different matter when they make changes to real infrastructure running production workloads. "Live infrastructure is unforgiving," Ang Chen, CEO of Vera Platforms and an associate professor at the University of Michigan, told The Register . "An incorrect change can take down a service, open a security hole or erase data. Mistakes are often irreversible, and there’s no safe way to experiment: running code against production infra just to see what happens isn’t an option." For the past few years, Chen and his colleagues have been working on a way to benchmark agentic DevOps and a gym – a simulation environment – to help AI models get better at DevOps tasks. "From the research that we did, we've figured out various weaknesses of leading models," said Chen. "For instance, [Anthropic's] Claude, although it's very strong with Python generation, it just has some fundamental limitations that it can't get right when it comes to DevOps." An example of that, Chen said, is that when they asked Claude or OpenAI's Codex to decommission resources in the AWS cloud, the models didn't look beyond the default region. "The default region is us-east-1," he explained. "There are various regions in AWS, but Claude doesn't have this awareness that the cloud resources could exist in multiple regions, so it only decommissioned part of the resource." The fundamental reason, he said, is that these models have seen a lot of public code, but a lot less operational tracing. Vera Platforms aims to remedy the situation with three products: vera-gym, a playground environment that emulates production infrastructure; vera-bench, a test for measuring where AI agents fumble DevOps tasks; and vera-agents, AI agents that have been trained in vera-gym and are ready to be deployed for DevOps tasks. The CloudOpsBench test being released builds upon work done in 2024 that was presented at NeurIPS. According to Chen, Claude and Codex only score about a 50 percent pass rate. "It's a very, very hard set of tasks," he said. The test covers tasks like deleting decommissioned S3 buckets , repairing a compliance event pipeline , and restoring DynamoDB write autoscaling . "The tasks are authored by senior infra operators with many years of experience, with rigorous peer review," said Chen. This benchmark has the advantage of not requiring an actual cloud deployment. "We have a high fidelity simulator that mimics Amazon behavior," said Chen. "So the rollout, the performance of the agent on the real cloud and the performance of the agent in our emulator is exactly the same. So for every API, we have this comparis

"For instance, [Anthropic's] Claude, although it's very strong with Python generation, it just has some fundamental limitations that it can't get right when it comes to DevOps." An example of that, Chen said, is that when they asked Claude or OpenAI's Codex to decommission resources in the AWS cloud, the models didn't look beyond the default region. "The default region is us-east-1," he explained. "There are various regions in AWS, but Claude doesn't have this awareness that the cloud resources could exist in multiple regions, so it only decommissioned part of the resource." The fundamental reason, he said, is that these models have seen a lot of public code, but a lot less operational tracing. Vera Platforms aims to remedy the situation with three products: vera-gym, a playground environment that emulates production infrastructure; vera-bench, a test for measuring where AI agents fumble DevOps tasks; and vera-agents, AI agents that have been trained in vera-gym and are ready to be deployed for DevOps tasks. The CloudOpsBench test being released builds upon work done in 2024 that was presented at NeurIPS. According to Chen, Claude and Codex only score about a 50 percent pass rate. "It's a very, very hard set of tasks," he said. The test covers tasks like deleting decommissioned S3 buckets , repairing a compliance event pipeline , and restoring DynamoDB write autoscaling . "The tasks are authored by senior infra operators with many years of experience, with rigorous peer review," said Chen. This benchmark has the advantage of not requiring an actual cloud deployment. "We have a high fidelity simulator that mimics Amazon behavior," said Chen. "So the rollout, the performance of the agent on the real cloud and the performance of the agent in our emulator is exactly the same. So for every API, we have this comparison and the agent sees the same thing." Vera-agents, Chen said, should be available in Q1 2027. In their academic work, the researchers describe cloud infrastructure as "critical but tedious work." With a bit more training, maybe AI agents can take over and keep things boring. ®

item.title: Money, Fashion & a Little Attitude! Ayra Starr and Theodora’s “Ms. Paper” Video Has It All
item.description: Ayra Starr wears a pink mini dress and side cap in the official “Ms. Paper” music video. Money, fashion, a little attitude, and Ayra Starr ? Oh, we’re definitely watching! The Starrgirl has just dropped the official music video for “ Ms. Paper ,” her collaboration with French rapper Theodora , and the two are having a lot of fun with this one. Taken from Ayra’s album Starrgirl, the fan-favourite track now has a colourful visual to match its playful lyrics. Produced by The Elements, “Ms. Paper” brings together Afropop rhythms and a catchy mix of English and French as Ayra and Theodora sing about making their own money, enjoying their success, and doing things on their own terms. And with a chorus that goes, “Moi, c’est Miss Kitoko ou Miss Paper,” you can already imagine how much fun the music video was going to be. So, what does being Ms. Paper look like? Apparently, it involves plenty of fashion, money, and a little pop-art fun. The video plays around with currency-inspired graphics, retro magazine covers, and custom toy-box packaging, giving Ayra and Theodora their own colourful world to play in. Ayra appears in a pink mini dress with a matching side cap and cowrie shell details before switching things up in a rich blue halter top, bright red hair, and striking face detailing. And there’s still more to enjoy. Between the money-counting scenes, museum-style portrait frames, and choreography, the video keeps finding new ways to bring the song’s playful mood to life. With Ayra Starr and Theodora moving between languages, fashion, and music, “Ms. Paper” is another fun addition to the Starrgirl era. Watch below The post Money, Fashion & a Little Attitude! Ayra Starr and Theodora’s “Ms. Paper” Video Has It All appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Topcoat enables Rust to render server-side web apps
item.description: Popular for other uses, Rust isn't typically deployed for web development. That could change, however. With AI here to do the heavy lifting, coders may want to consider the programming language, given its runtime performance and safety guarantees, suggested Carl Lerche , an Amazon Web Services principal engineer, speaking at ScyllaDB’s 2026 P99 virtual conference last week. Lerche was there to demonstrate his latest project, Topcoat , a framework for running web applications written in Rust. Lerche is perhaps best known for creating Tokio , which is the most popular asynchronous Rust runtime in that ecosystem. “Three years ago, had [I] gone out and said that Rust could be the best language for building web apps, you probably would have called me crazy,” he told the virtual audience. Web developers gravitate towards the languages they find most familiar. These days, that means JavaScript, or possibly Ruby. A number of web frameworks already use Rust. Both Leptos and Dioxus compile Rust into WebAssembly, which most browsers run. This approach is great for heavy computational jobs, though the upfront loading time can be a real drag. Topcoat compiles your Rust code into more web-friendly JavaScript. For Lerche, JavaScript remains the best way to interact with the browser's Document Object Model (DOM). “Generally, the approach taken by any Rust framework can be traced back to another ecosystem, usually a very popular one. You can't really point to a single existing framework as [Topcoat’s] main source of inspiration,” noted frontend developer Ken Kohlman, in a summary video on his “Code to the Moon” YouTube channel. Walk on the server side Lerche admitted that Topcoat isn’t for building complex applications, on the scale of, say, Figma, but it can easily be used for the run-of-the-mill, browser-based, database-driven applications, which is to say 90 percent of the web today. Unlike most present-day JavaScript frameworks , Topcoat eschews the current definition of being reactive, where the program logic is dumped onto the browser when the session begins. Instead, most of the logic executes on the server, with only the results delivered to the browser (Developers can still write client-side logic using a subset of Rust, which Topcoat automatically compiles into JavaScript for the browser). It’s an old idea recast with better tech. Server-side rendering predates reactive programming (see Apache’s server-side includes ). With server-side rendering, Lerche admitted, “It might sound like we're going back to the old days of full page refreshes for every click [but] you can actually get almost all of what you think of as reactive with server-side rendering.” But server-side programming has been making a comeback lately, especially for those devs disgruntled with React and other frameworks. item.dc:creator: Joab Jackson
item.content:encoded: Popular for other uses, Rust isn't typically deployed for web development. That could change, however. With AI here to do the heavy lifting, coders may want to consider the programming language, given its runtime performance and safety guarantees, suggested Carl Lerche , an Amazon Web Services principal engineer, speaking at ScyllaDB’s 2026 P99 virtual conference last week. Lerche was there to demonstrate his latest project, Topcoat , a framework for running web applications written in Rust. Lerche is perhaps best known for creating Tokio , which is the most popular asynchronous Rust runtime in that ecosystem. “Three years ago, had [I] gone out and said that Rust could be the best language for building web apps, you probably would have called me crazy,” he told the virtual audience. Web developers gravitate towards the languages they find most familiar. These days, that means JavaScript, or possibly Ruby. A number of web frameworks already use Rust. Both Leptos and Dioxus compile Rust into WebAssembly, which most browsers run. This approach is great for heavy computational jobs, though the upfront loading time can be a real drag. Topcoat compiles your Rust code into more web-friendly JavaScript. For Lerche, JavaScript remains the best way to interact with the browser's Document Object Model (DOM). “Generally, the approach taken by any Rust framework can be traced back to another ecosystem, usually a very popular one. You can't really point to a single existing framework as [Topcoat’s] main source of inspiration,” noted frontend developer Ken Kohlman, in a summary video on his “Code to the Moon” YouTube channel. Walk on the server side Lerche admitted that Topcoat isn’t for building complex applications, on the scale of, say, Figma, but it can easily be used for the run-of-the-mill, browser-based, database-driven applications, which is to say 90 percent of the web today. Unlike most present-day JavaScript frameworks , Topcoat eschews the current definition of being reactive, where the program logic is dumped onto the browser when the session begins. Instead, most of the logic executes on the server, with only the results delivered to the browser (Developers can still write client-side logic using a subset of Rust, which Topcoat automatically compiles into JavaScript for the browser). It’s an old idea recast with better tech. Server-side rendering predates reactive programming (see Apache’s server-side includes ). With server-side rendering, Lerche admitted, “It might sound like we're going back to the old days of full page refreshes for every click [but] you can actually get almost all of what you think of as reactive with server-side rendering.” But server-side programming has been making a comeback lately, especially for those devs disgruntled with React and other frameworks. HTMX , Datastar , and Phoenix LiveView all render web pages on the server, sending them back to the browser nearly completed. Topcoat is just tweaking their ideas to fit well with Rust, Lerche said. When a user smashes a button on a web page, the whole page isn’t refreshed. Just the HTML snippet for that component is returned and refreshed by the server. JavaScript in the front, Rust in the back Topcoat saves load times by rendering all the components at once, rather than one by one. Also, data loading does not block the loading of the page. The server can send back a web page with placeholders into which the data will stream. One big dollop of secret sauce that Topcoat has is that it provides a way for the component, which is already on the server, to speak directly to the database, thanks to an earlier project from Lerche called Toasty , a Rust-based asynchronous database object-relational mapper (which he spoke about at P99 2024). “You can do your rendering right with the data immediately, so you don't have to figure out how to serialize it, send it to the client, deserialize it,” he said. By pushing data loading deep down into the page render, the server can send the head of the HTML template to the client immediately, allowing the browser to start preloading assets (like CSS or images) while the server renders the rest of the page. “The simplicity is incredible, and it is something that we have been sorely missing in this space. I feel like someone who doesn't really know Rust could get off the ground pretty quickly with this thing,” Kohlman said. He did agree with Lerche that Topcoat is best for smaller web projects, given that Topcoat only uses a subset of the Rust syntax. “There's something to be said for having the full Rust syntax at your disposal,” he said. ®

item.title: Suspected Chinese attackers built a custom PHP2Shell exploit and rooted 25 servers
item.description: Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, according to Dream researchers. The snoops began exploiting these servers on October 23, targeting organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The attackers also honed in on US government-affiliated firewalls. “Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign - all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet,” the Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said in a report. Plus, the attackers “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks, Dream noted. The attackers rooted the first US government-affiliated firewall on October 23, but the device crashed shortly afterward, possibly due to around 900 MB of exploit traffic. According to Dream, it remained unresponsive despite 240 automated checks over two hours. They successfully exploited the second firewall a day later, on October 24. The compromised firewalls ran vulnerable versions of Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS. Dream said it had been working with the vendor to investigate the compromises, and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 researchers independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed Dream's reported results. To break into the firewalls, the attackers built a custom exploit chain that includes PHP2Shell and a Fragnesia kernel flaw, and ran about 40 custom post-exploitation scripts once they were inside the targeted organizations. Total attack chain in under 15 minutes PHP2Shell , comprised of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, came to light early last week, along with fears that attackers would abuse the bugs to take down most of the internet . Despite “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, the first reports of successful attacks didn’t start until Saturday. Both bugs have CVSS scores of 9.2 and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. The PHP2Shell exploit recovered by Dream was not a copy of any known public exploit. It “appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform,” the researchers wrote. The attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia ( CVE-2026-46300 ), a high-severity local privilege-escalation vulnerability affecting the Linux kernel's XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added this Linux kernel bug to its catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities on Wednesday. Both CISA and the FBI declined to comment. The attackers also honed in on US government-affiliated firewalls. “Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign - all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet,” the Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said in a report. Plus, the attackers “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks, Dream noted. The attackers rooted the first US government-affiliated firewall on October 23, but the device crashed shortly afterward, possibly due to around 900 MB of exploit traffic. According to Dream, it remained unresponsive despite 240 automated checks over two hours. They successfully exploited the second firewall a day later, on October 24. The compromised firewalls ran vulnerable versions of Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS. Dream said it had been working with the vendor to investigate the compromises, and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 researchers independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed Dream's reported results. To break into the firewalls, the attackers built a custom exploit chain that includes PHP2Shell and a Fragnesia kernel flaw, and ran about 40 custom post-exploitation scripts once they were inside the targeted organizations. Total attack chain in under 15 minutes PHP2Shell , comprised of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, came to light early last week, along with fears that attackers would abuse the bugs to take down most of the internet . Despite “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, the first reports of successful attacks didn’t start until Saturday. Both bugs have CVSS scores of 9.2 and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. The PHP2Shell exploit recovered by Dream was not a copy of any known public exploit. It “appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform,” the researchers wrote. The attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia ( CVE-2026-46300 ), a high-severity local privilege-escalation vulnerability affecting the Linux kernel's XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added this Linux kernel bug to its catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities on Wednesday. Both CISA and the FBI declined to comment. The miscreants developed a four-stage PHP2Shell exploit that allowed them to execute commands without authentication on vulnerable Palo Alto Networks firewalls. They then used Fragnesia to escalate their privileges and gain root access. The attackers targeted PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2, which run PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enabled the exploit's memory-corruption stages. “The total chain - from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell - completes in under 15 minutes,” the Dream team wrote. 4 steps to root Here’s how it works: First, they flood the servers with crafted multipart POST requests to corrupt PHP’s memory, and force a predictable memory layout. Then a second request forges the stale session ID length from the memory corruption part of the attack, forcing an out-of-bounds read and exposing the base address of libphp.so in the running process. The attackers then exhaust PHP's memory again to force mod_data=NULL, creating a stale reference they can forge in the final stage to execute commands as the nobody user. They use Fragnesia to escalate to root and plant a web shell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall. After breaking in via the compromised firewalls, the attackers snooped around in Active Directory, stealing credentials and other sensitive information. With root access, the attackers also had the master key to decrypt the LDAP service account password, which they hardcoded into every subsequent script. They also enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries, and sprayed passwords against every user account. Attackers also tried to create backdoor AD accounts and attempted SAML signing key extraction - but Dream doesn’t know if these were successful. “The attack results - whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted - stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered,” the researchers noted. AI tools in the attack The investigation also uncovered evidence that the attackers used AI tools, but noted that this was not a fully autonomous attack. The researchers found Anthropic's Claude Code installed, an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with Chinese models DeepSeek and Kimi, and API keys for the FOFA reconnaissance service. FOFA is a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan. The attackers used it to identify about 19,000 internet-facing Palo Alto Networks firewalls worldwide. “The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running,” Dream warned. “And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional PAN-OS versions.”®

item.title: See NASA's Artemis III astronauts meet Trump at the White House as they train for a critical 2027 moon lander test flight (photos)
item.description: null U.S. President Donald Trump just met another NASA Artemis crew. The astronauts of NASA's Artemis III mission visited the Oval Office on Thursday (Oct. 28) and posed for a few photos with the president. Their visit came nearly six months to the day after that of the Artemis II crew, who stopped by the White House on April 29 , 19 days after the end of their historic flight around the moon . President Trump talks to the Artemis III crew on Oct. 28, 2026. (Image credit: The White House) The Artemis III astronauts are NASA's Randy Bresnik (commander), Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio (mission specialists) and the European Space Agency 's Luca Parmitano (pilot). All four — plus backup crewmate Bob Hines of NASA, and agency chief Jared Isaacman — made the White House trip. "It was a great day at the White House with President Trump and the talented crew of Artemis III," Isaacman wrote via X on Thursday . Artemis III will launch to low Earth orbit in the summer of 2027, if all goes according to plan. The roughly two-week-long mission will aim to dock NASA's Orion capsule with SpaceX's Starship vehicle and/or Blue Origin's Blue Moon . NASA selected Starship and Blue Moon to be the crewed lunar landers for the Artemis program , so Artemis III will provide valuable practice : On moon-landing missions, astronauts will launch aboard Orion and then meet up with either Starship or Blue Moon, which will carry them to the lunar surface and back up again. That's slated to happen for the first time on Artemis IV, which NASA plans to launch in 2028 . We don't yet know which private lander(s) will launch on Artemis III; NASA would like to fly both of them, but it's unclear if both will be ready when the time comes. That uncertainty applies to Artemis IV as well. We'll have to wait a bit before we know which spacecraft will have the honor of putting astronauts down on the moon for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972.

These products are centred around two product series; is is anchored by two hero product series. First are the Vita Luxe premium comfort mattress and the Vita Helix hybrid foam-and-spring mattress. They are standard mattresses designed to bring the best of mattress technology to Nigerian homes. Vitafoam also introduced the Mattress- in-a-Box series, two products, Vita Restora and Vita Compresso , as well as VitaCool Plus pillow, which brings the best of global engineering technology into the Nigerian market – the only company currently manufacturing this in the country. Here are 10 things you need to know about the Luxury Collection and mattress-in-a-box technology. 01 It’s a whole new premium range, not a single product The Vitafoam Luxury Collection presents a complete range of premium mattresses, not one new model. It is the brand’s most ambitious push into premium sleep in years, and a clear signal that ‘everyday luxury’ is no longer reserved for imported names. 02 Two flagships lead it: Vita Luxe and Vita Helix Vita Luxe is the top of the range, deep, cradling premium comfort that gives an ordinary night the feel of a five-star hotel. Vita Helix is the premium hybrid: foam layers over a responsive spring system, engineered for support that lasts. Together, they anchor the collection. 03 Two signature products, a brand-new mattress-in-a-box range Alongside the luxury line, Vitafoam has launched a mattress-in-a-box range: the premium hybrid Vita Restora and the convenient Vita Compresso . Both are engineered and compressed locally, so a full-size mattress can be delivered to your door in a package that can easily be transported. 04 Yes, Mattress-in-a-box means a full mattress really comes rolled up in a box It sounds like a trick, but it is simple engineering. The Vitafoam Website contains lot of products within its standard range of products. The Luxury Collection also covers every stage of life. Vita Compresso suits the first apartment or a fresh start. Vita Restora fits the home you are building. Vita Helix is for couples and high performers. Vita Luxe is for when you have truly arrived. Wherever you are, whatever your sleeping style, there is a Vitafoam made for it. 10 The bigger idea: Vitafoam wants you to rest well so you can live fully Beneath the products is a point of view. In a country that celebrates hustle, Vitafoam is making the case that you cannot live fully if you do not rest well. And that proper rest is not a reward for success, but the foundation of it. You deserve to have the flex of the fine art of living. The Vitafoam Luxury Collection and Mattress-in-a-box range are available. You can either visit the comfort centres or order the Vita Cool Plus pillow , Vita Compresso, or Vita Restora via the Vitafoam website and have it delivered to you (in some selected states). item.title: Birds can get jet lag on long, fast flights and then fly off course
item.description: A Manx shearwater in flight low over the sea, near Wales Nature Picture Library / Alamy Stock Photo You don’t need a jet plane to get jet lag – even feathers will do. At least one species of bird gets jet lag, in the sense that its body clock can diverge from local time by more than an hour on fast flights across the Atlantic, as revealed by navigational errors. “We’ve slightly shied away from using the term jet lag itself, because people associate that with the health impacts of that clock shift, rather than the clock shift itself. But it’s exactly the same process that causes jet lag in people,” says Patrick Lewin at the University of Oxford. “It’s having these physiological and behavioural effects, where the birds are mistiming their behaviours.” It is likely that other long-distance fliers, possibly including some insects and bats as well as birds, also get jet lag in the clock-shift sense, says Lewin. Advertisement Read more Birds wearing tiny trackers reveal migration routes in amazing detail Manx shearwaters are small seabirds that fly vast distances, using a technique called dynamic soaring to exploit wind gradients near the sea surface. “They’ve evolved this niche of being really amazing long-distance travellers,” says Lewin. They breed on islands around the UK and Ireland . While parents are raising a chick , they may fly more than 1000 kilometres westwards to reach rich fishing grounds in the mid-Atlantic. Once they have food, they fly back in a fairly straight line, diverting only to skirt around landmasses such as Ireland. How do they achieve these navigational feats ? While some birds can sense Earth’s magnetic field, Manx shearwaters don’t appear to. Lewin’s team has confirmed this by attaching small magnets to the birds that should disrupt geomagnetic navigation. They had no effect . Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter Instead, it appears that shearwaters rely on a sun compass – if you know what time it is, you can maintain a course by adjusting your orientation relative to the sun . Many animals, from insects and fish to turtles and birds, have been shown to do this. If their internal clocks are reset using artificial light and darkness, they head in the wrong direction. “We realised that there might be a kind of natural experiment where the birds were manipulating their own clocks,” says Lewin. For instance, at 6am, a Manx shearwater wanting to fly eastwards back to its nest needs to head sunwards. At noon, it needs to fly at right angles to the sun, which will be due south. But if a shearwater travels 15° of longitude eastwards, the local time will be 1pm, while its internal clock will still register the time as noon, so the sun will no longer be due south. This means birds flying rapidly east should veer slightly off course in a clockwise direction over the course of day, in the absence of other cues. item.content:encoded: A Manx shearwater in flight low over the sea, near Wales Nature Picture Library / Alamy Stock Photo You don’t need a jet plane to get jet lag – even feathers will do. At least one species of bird gets jet lag, in the sense that its body clock can diverge from local time by more than an hour on fast flights across the Atlantic, as revealed by navigational errors. “We’ve slightly shied away from using the term jet lag itself, because people associate that with the health impacts of that clock shift, rather than the clock shift itself. But it’s exactly the same process that causes jet lag in people,” says Patrick Lewin at the University of Oxford. “It’s having these physiological and behavioural effects, where the birds are mistiming their behaviours.” It is likely that other long-distance fliers, possibly including some insects and bats as well as birds, also get jet lag in the clock-shift sense, says Lewin. Advertisement Read more Birds wearing tiny trackers reveal migration routes in amazing detail Manx shearwaters are small seabirds that fly vast distances, using a technique called dynamic soaring to exploit wind gradients near the sea surface. “They’ve evolved this niche of being really amazing long-distance travellers,” says Lewin. They breed on islands around the UK and Ireland . While parents are raising a chick , they may fly more than 1000 kilometres westwards to reach rich fishing grounds in the mid-Atlantic. Once they have food, they fly back in a fairly straight line, diverting only to skirt around landmasses such as Ireland. How do they achieve these navigational feats ? While some birds can sense Earth’s magnetic field, Manx shearwaters don’t appear to. Lewin’s team has confirmed this by attaching small magnets to the birds that should disrupt geomagnetic navigation. They had no effect . Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter Instead, it appears that shearwaters rely on a sun compass – if you know what time it is, you can maintain a course by adjusting your orientation relative to the sun . Many animals, from insects and fish to turtles and birds, have been shown to do this. If their internal clocks are reset using artificial light and darkness, they head in the wrong direction. “We realised that there might be a kind of natural experiment where the birds were manipulating their own clocks,” says Lewin. For instance, at 6am, a Manx shearwater wanting to fly eastwards back to its nest needs to head sunwards. At noon, it needs to fly at right angles to the sun, which will be due south. But if a shearwater travels 15° of longitude eastwards, the local time will be 1pm, while its internal clock will still register the time as noon, so the sun will no longer be due south. This means birds flying rapidly east should veer slightly off course in a clockwise direction over the course of day, in the absence of other cues. Read more Australian moths use the stars as a compass on 1000-km migrations Other researchers have been attaching GPS trackers to Manx shearwaters for decades, so the paths taken on nearly 4000 foraging trips are known. Sure enough, when Lewin and his colleagues analysed these flight tracks, they found birds on rapid return flights tended to deviate clockwise when out of sight of land. The team considered other potential explanations, from the Coriolis effect to winds. “The one thing that best predicted the observed changes in shearwaters’ orientation was always this sun compass effect,” says Lewin. The effect is small. After a 1000 km flight, a bird would have to fly only an extra 5 km to reach its colony, which, for such efficient long-distance fliers, is probably negligible, Lewin says. This might explain why Manx shearwaters haven’t evolved some mechanism for avoiding jet lag , he says. Flight Paths review: Why understanding migration may save bird species Solving the mysteries of bird migration with technology not only unlocks unexpected secrets but is crucial to conservation efforts, says Rebecca Heisman in her fascinating first book “What is good about the study is that they analyse a lot of tracks, making for robust data to test different models,” says Ken Cheng at Macquarie University in Sydney. While other species may get this form of jet lag, too, long-distance flights by birds are typically done during migrations, and migrations usually involve mainly north-south travel, says Cheng, so jet lag won’t be much of a problem. However, near the poles, the travel distance required to cross 15° or more of longitude becomes so short that many animals might be affected, says Lewin, perhaps even including polar bears or Arctic foxes travelling on sea ice. “Near-polar species may be quite strongly affected,” he says. “Now, it all gets a bit complicated because you have 24-hour daylight and 24-hour darkness in parts of the year, so circadian rhythms break down generally in some species.” Journal Reference: Science DOI: 10.1126/science.adz2542

item.title: Cosmic graveyard of zombie planets offers a grisly warning about our own solar system's fate
item.description: null "Sometimes dead is better." Who can forget the immortal words of Jud Crandall, delivered by the incomparable Fred Gwynne in the 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's Pet Sematary? Turns out Crandall could have been talking about somewhere just as otherworldly as the cursed Chumash burial ground at the heart of one of King's most terrifying works of fiction. That's because astronomers have discovered two husks of two zombie planets shuffling through the gory remains of what was once their planetary neighbors around a long-deceased star, or white dwarf. The shattered planets were revealed by a clear gap in the debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, located around 1,600 light-years away from Earth. One of the remnants is estimated to be no larger than the size of the average solar system asteroid, while the other is estimated to be between the size of the moon and the dwarf planet Pluto. If this wasn't creepy enough, this haunting planetary system could be a grisly warning about the future of our own solar system after the inevitable death of the sun. White dwarfs like the one at the heart of this system are formed when stars around the same mass as the sun run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means they can no longer fuse hydrogen into helium, the nuclear fusion process that provides the outward push that supports a star against the inward push of its own gravity. As a result, the stars' cores collapse while the outer layers, where nuclear fusion is still proceeding, puff out. This so-called red giant phase can see stars increase their radius by many 100s of times. When it happens to the sun in around 5 billion years, our star will expand to consume the inner planets, including Earth. The red giant phase ends when the outer layers disperse along with the wreckage of consumed planets, leaving a smoldering stellar core, now a white dwarf, surrounded by the disk-shaped remains of its outer layers and cannibalized planetary children. But this may not be the final death of all the planets that once orbited the now-dead star. "We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," research leader Nicola Gentille Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste, Italy, said in a statement. Violent stellar death can't kill these two planetary Jason Voorhees This system differs from others seen because of the large gap between the remarkably stable inner and outer rings. All previously known debris discs around white dwarfs have been surrounded by single, flat, rotating disks, not a double structure like this. "The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," team member Gentle Fusillo of the Astronomical Observat

item.content:encoded: null "Sometimes dead is better." Who can forget the immortal words of Jud Crandall, delivered by the incomparable Fred Gwynne in the 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's Pet Sematary? Turns out Crandall could have been talking about somewhere just as otherworldly as the cursed Chumash burial ground at the heart of one of King's most terrifying works of fiction. That's because astronomers have discovered two husks of two zombie planets shuffling through the gory remains of what was once their planetary neighbors around a long-deceased star, or white dwarf. The shattered planets were revealed by a clear gap in the debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, located around 1,600 light-years away from Earth. One of the remnants is estimated to be no larger than the size of the average solar system asteroid, while the other is estimated to be between the size of the moon and the dwarf planet Pluto. If this wasn't creepy enough, this haunting planetary system could be a grisly warning about the future of our own solar system after the inevitable death of the sun. White dwarfs like the one at the heart of this system are formed when stars around the same mass as the sun run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means they can no longer fuse hydrogen into helium, the nuclear fusion process that provides the outward push that supports a star against the inward push of its own gravity. As a result, the stars' cores collapse while the outer layers, where nuclear fusion is still proceeding, puff out. This so-called red giant phase can see stars increase their radius by many 100s of times. When it happens to the sun in around 5 billion years, our star will expand to consume the inner planets, including Earth. The red giant phase ends when the outer layers disperse along with the wreckage of consumed planets, leaving a smoldering stellar core, now a white dwarf, surrounded by the disk-shaped remains of its outer layers and cannibalized planetary children. But this may not be the final death of all the planets that once orbited the now-dead star. "We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," research leader Nicola Gentille Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste, Italy, said in a statement. Violent stellar death can't kill these two planetary Jason Voorhees This system differs from others seen because of the large gap between the remarkably stable inner and outer rings. All previously known debris discs around white dwarfs have been surrounded by single, flat, rotating disks, not a double structure like this. "The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," team member Gentle Fusillo of the Astronomical Observatory of Trieste said. The team thinks that this unique double structure is evidence of planets that weren't completely vaporized during this white dwarf's red giant phase. That means just like the residents and campers of Crystal Lake couldn't finish off Pamela Voorhees' baby boy, even an expanding star couldn't finish these two planets. An illustration shows a massive black hole seed next to a standard stellar mass black hole (Image credit: Fortuna and Gentile Fusillo) The team's observations, made with the Very Large Telescope (VLT), revealed the presence of calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron in the disk around the white dwarf. This indicates the destroyed planets had a composition similar to the rocky planets of the inner solar system. The researchers also found evidence of a diversity of composition in the destroyed planets. The chemistry of the outer rings deviated from that of the inner rings, indicating that at least two of the consumed planets had very different compositions. "The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like," Lagos-Vilches explained. The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

item.title: AWIEF and Open Society Foundations Champion Women-Led Enterprises for Peace and Security in Africa at AWIEF 2026
item.description: The Africa Women Innovation and Entrepreneurship Forum (AWIEF) is pleased to announce its partnership with Open Society Foundations (OSF) for AWIEF 2026 , taking place on 10 and 11 November 2026 at the Cape Town International Convention Centre (CTICC). The annual AWIEF Conference, currently in its twelfth edition, is a flagship convening of entrepreneurs, investors, corporates, government, and development partners from across Africa and beyond. The partnership will take center stage during the opening plenary, Peace Dividends: Why Women-Led Enterprise Is a Security Strategy, Not Just an Economic One , exploring how women entrepreneurs contribute to economic stability, rebuild trust in communities affected by conflict, and help create the foundations for lasting peace. Across fragile and post-conflict regions, from the Sahel to the Great Lakes and the Horn of Africa, women entrepreneurs play a vital role in restoring livelihoods and rebuilding local markets. Yet their contribution to peace building and security remains overlooked and unsung. The plenary will examine how women-led businesses can strengthen community resilience, alongside the need for more effective access to capital, supportive policies and funding systems that empower their role in peace and development. Opening Plenary: Peace Dividends The discussion will be moderated by Idil Absiaye, Regional Head of Women, Peace and Security (WPS) Policy at UN Women , and feature: Aimée Ongeso , Program Manager, Transformative Peace, Open Society Foundations. Ibrahim Mulushewa Eshete , Co-Founder and Executive Director, Center for National and Regional Integration Studies (CeNRIS), Ethiopia. Amb. Ninikanwa O. Okey-Uche, Consul General, Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, Johannesburg. Yvette Mwanza, CEO of Kivu Mineral Resources and President of the North Kivu Chamber of Mines, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Bringing together perspectives from peace building, regional integration, diplomacy and business, the panel will explore what is working on the ground and what needs to change to better support women-led enterprises as contributors to peace and security. Through this partnership, AWIEF and OSF will spotlight the connection between women’s economic empowerment, resilient communities and sustainable peace, reinforcing the importance of recognizing women entrepreneurs as not only drivers of economic growth, but also contributors to stability across Africa. The opening plenary takes place on 10 November 2026 at the CTICC, Cape Town, as part of AWIEF 2026. Registration and tickets for AWIEF 2026 Conference are available online at: https://www.awieforum.org/purchase-conference-tickets/#tickets About AWIEF AWIEF is a leading pan-African organisation advancing women’s economic inclusion through entrepreneurship, innovation and business leadership. item.content:encoded: The Africa Women Innovation and Entrepreneurship Forum (AWIEF) is pleased to announce its partnership with Open Society Foundations (OSF) for AWIEF 2026 , taking place on 10 and 11 November 2026 at the Cape Town International Convention Centre (CTICC). The annual AWIEF Conference, currently in its twelfth edition, is a flagship convening of entrepreneurs, investors, corporates, government, and development partners from across Africa and beyond. The partnership will take center stage during the opening plenary, Peace Dividends: Why Women-Led Enterprise Is a Security Strategy, Not Just an Economic One , exploring how women entrepreneurs contribute to economic stability, rebuild trust in communities affected by conflict, and help create the foundations for lasting peace. Across fragile and post-conflict regions, from the Sahel to the Great Lakes and the Horn of Africa, women entrepreneurs play a vital role in restoring livelihoods and rebuilding local markets. Yet their contribution to peace building and security remains overlooked and unsung. The plenary will examine how women-led businesses can strengthen community resilience, alongside the need for more effective access to capital, supportive policies and funding systems that empower their role in peace and development. Opening Plenary: Peace Dividends The discussion will be moderated by Idil Absiaye, Regional Head of Women, Peace and Security (WPS) Policy at UN Women , and feature: Aimée Ongeso , Program Manager, Transformative Peace, Open Society Foundations. Ibrahim Mulushewa Eshete , Co-Founder and Executive Director, Center for National and Regional Integration Studies (CeNRIS), Ethiopia. Amb. Ninikanwa O. Okey-Uche, Consul General, Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, Johannesburg. Yvette Mwanza, CEO of Kivu Mineral Resources and President of the North Kivu Chamber of Mines, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Bringing together perspectives from peace building, regional integration, diplomacy and business, the panel will explore what is working on the ground and what needs to change to better support women-led enterprises as contributors to peace and security. Through this partnership, AWIEF and OSF will spotlight the connection between women’s economic empowerment, resilient communities and sustainable peace, reinforcing the importance of recognizing women entrepreneurs as not only drivers of economic growth, but also contributors to stability across Africa. The opening plenary takes place on 10 November 2026 at the CTICC, Cape Town, as part of AWIEF 2026. Registration and tickets for AWIEF 2026 Conference are available online at: https://www.awieforum.org/purchase-conference-tickets/#tickets About AWIEF AWIEF is a leading pan-African organisation advancing women’s economic inclusion through entrepreneurship, innovation and business leadership. Established since 2015, AWIEF has directly supported more than 6,500 female founders and entrepreneurs with enterprise development programs, training, and mentorship while facilitating access to finance, markets, and networks. About Open Society Foundations OSF supports individuals and organisations working to advance more just, inclusive and accountable societies. Media enquiries AWIEF Communications Team Email: info@awieforum.org Website: www.awieforum.org AWIEF 2026 | 10–11 November 2026 | CTICC, Cape Town, South Africa BellaNaija is a Media Partner for AWIEF The post AWIEF and Open Society Foundations Champion Women-Led Enterprises for Peace and Security in Africa at AWIEF 2026 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Ubuntu 27.04 may bring a preview of the long-awaited Core Desktop
item.description: It's a few years behind schedule, but development has resumed on the desktop edition of Canonical's existing immutable IoT distro, Ubuntu Core. Engineering veep Jon Seager announced that Canonical is Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop on the company's Discourse forum. Even before his announcement, there was some fresh activity on the project's GitHub . The post gives some explanation of why the effort is running so late, envisions three potential use cases, and talks a little about the work that is already going on to enable it to finally happen. There's no solid timeline given, but Seager says that "over the coming release cycle" the team will be working out what needs to happen, which means that "over the coming weeks, we'll have the infrastructure ready for… daily image builds for Ubuntu Core Desktop." "Accelerating" sounds good, but with the best will in the world, it could hardly slow it down. In mid-2023 it looked like Desktop Ubuntu Core would arrive in 2024 , and at that year's Ubuntu Summit in Rīga, Latvia, it revealed more details . At the 2024 Summit, there was a talk about a KDE version – but no release. At the 2025 Summit, the Reg FOSS desk interviewed Seager and "Where's Core Desktop?" was our first question. The three roles his post discusses are the "browser-centric machine", a "developer workstation," and a "gaming machine." For this vulture, these goals imply two separate things. In general, this seems to indicate that it's wary of making something too specialized early on, then finding that it's not versatile enough for more challenging roles. Secondly, we think that the company is thinking of three specific niches that rival immutable distros have occupied successfully for years. Right now, the "browser-centric" one is filled by ChromeOS and ChromeOS Flex . We use Flex – it's pretty good, even if its days are now numbered due to the new Android-based GooglebookOS . Secondly, Fedora's Atomic editions have been around for years now – The Register first mentioned Fedora Kinoite well over five years ago. As well as Fedoras's own versions , there are also community-led distros based on the same tech, called Universal Blue . We've tried several, and while for now they offer nothing much this vulture wants, they undeniably work and they have happy users. Fedora's marketing aims at developers, and an immutable distro with containerized environments on top is harder to accidentally break with crashy work-in-progress code. Thirdly, the games-machine niche is owned by Valve's SteamOS . Although it is native to the Steam Deck – and if you're among the lucky few, the Steam Machine and Steam Frame – you are also free to run this on your own AMD-based kit . All three of these product families have been well-established for between five to ten years now. Canonical is lagging behind, and this is a subtle acknowledgement that it knows who the leaders are.
